subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Satisficing vs. Maximizing
description: A quick, practical guide to Satisficing vs. Maximizing.

hook.text: She visited 30 apartments and chose none. Her friend visited 3 and was happy. Who decided better?

buildup.text: Herbert Simon coined 'satisficing': choosing the first option that meets your criteria, then stopping.

discovery.text: Maximizers search for the best possible option. Satisficers search for good enough. Satisficers are happier.

twist.text: Schwartz found maximizers earn more money but feel worse about their choices. More options, more regret.

climax.text: Define your minimum criteria before searching. When something meets them, choose it. Stop looking.

punchline.text: Good enough often beats the best.

quiz.question: What did Schwartz find about maximizers?
options: They are always happier with their choices
They earn more but feel worse about decisions

details.summary: Satisficing means choosing the first option that meets a minimum threshold of acceptability rather than exhaustively searching for the best possible option. Maximizers search for the optimal choice and often end up less satisfied than satisficers who settle for good enough.
details.whyItMatters: The paradox of choice shows that maximizing becomes increasingly costly as options multiply. Maximizers spend more time, feel more regret, and report lower satisfaction than satisficers who accept good enough, despite sometimes finding objectively.
takeaways: Satisficers accept the first option meeting their threshold and feel content
Maximizers search exhaustively and feel regret about possibly missing better options
More options make maximizing more costly while satisficing remains efficient

faq.question: Is satisficing just settling for mediocrity?
faq.answer: No. Satisficing sets clear standards and accepts the first option meeting them. The standards can be high. The key difference is stopping once a good option is found rather than continuing to search for the perfect one, which often does not exist.

faq.question: What determines whether someone is a maximizer or satisficer?
faq.answer: It is partly personality and partly domain-specific. Someone might satisfice for restaurants but maximize for career decisions. Research shows maximizers tend to achieve better objective outcomes but lower subjective satisfaction due to opportunity cost awareness.
